title: Token budget backpressure lab journal
content:
Summary:

This is a lab-journal for the "token-budget backpressure" experiments. The goal: reduce p99 tail latency under mixed-size workloads by giving the scheduler a lightweight notion of token budget per request and applying admission/backpressure rules so long-running requests don't monopolize batch formation. This is not a full fairness overhaul — it’s an incremental probe to see whether a token-budget heuristic + soft backpressure can improve tail without major throughput regressions.

Why this idea?
- Observed: heavy skew in per-request token demand (chat long responses vs short completions) amplifies tail latency because large requests keep early batches occupied and delay slot assignment for small, latency-sensitive requests.
- Hypothesis: If scheduler tracks a small integer token budget estimate per inflight request and uses it to shape admission and preemption, we can: (1) limit token monopolization, (2) improve p95/p99 for short jobs, (3) preserve aggregate throughput by allowing large jobs to be serviced with slightly higher latency but without blocking the system.

Quick implementation notes (prototype):
- Add 2 fields to request meta (passed in header): estimated_token_budget (int, optional), latency_priority (low|normal|high). For experiments we synthetic-instrumented clients to set budget from the prompt length + expected temperature multiplier.
- Scheduler hooks: when constructing a batch, prefer to take requests with remaining token_budget > 0 and penalize requests that have consumed more than their budget in the last second. If the queue is dominated by over-budget requests, start applying a soft delay (backoff) to their admission for up to 5ms (configurable).
- Preemption: implement a micro-evict-on-formation rule — if a new high-priority request arrives and the currently forming batch has >X tokens reserved to single long request, evict the long request back to head of queue (with a raised urgency flag) and fill the batch with smaller ones. Evicted requests are requeued with slight precedence to avoid starvation loops.

Experiment setups (driver):
- Cluster: 3 x p4d-ish machines in testbed with identical model shard config. CPU shim disabled. All runs used same model variant (redwood-70b-quant).
- Load generator: custom-driver v0.9.2 (fork of wrk2) generating Poisson arrivals; two-class workload: short (mean 8 tokens response) and long (mean 1,200 tokens response). Mix: 70% short, 30% long (to stress tail). Also ran 50/50 and 90/10 mixes for sensitivity.
- Workload profiles: steady arrival rates at 350 req/s (cluster limit ~370), burst tests (500 req/s for 30s), and microburst trains (pulses of 100ms at 2–3x baseline).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (total server side), tokens/sec, average batch size (requests and tokens), queue length distribution, fairness metric = mean slowdown (resp latency/solo latency) per class, headroom (unused batch capacity), and preemption counts.

Baseline (no token budget, current hybrid-coalescer):
- Steady 350 rps, 70/30 mix: p50=38ms, p95=212ms, p99=1,125ms, throughput = stable at 360 rps. Average batch size = 6 requests / 4.2k tokens. Preemption events negligible.

Variant A: conservative token-budget (per-request budget = estimated_response_tokens * 1.2, soft-delay up to 2ms)
- p50=40ms, p95=190ms (-10%), p99=860ms (-24%). Throughput -1.8%. Avg batch size (requests) = 5.8, avg tokens=3.9k. Preemptions: 14 per minute (small). Fairness (mean slowdown): short=1.12, long=1.45 (baseline short=1.18 long=1.38).
- Notes: Short class improved at p99 significantly; long class took slightly higher latency (expected). Overall cost (tokens/sec) similar.

Variant B: aggressive backpressure (soft-delay up to 6ms + stricter budget accounting, evict large holders more often)
- p50=42ms, p95=175ms (-17%), p99=690ms (-39%). Throughput -4.1% (more batches with wasted slots). Avg batch size (requests) = 5.2, avg tokens=3.6k. Preemptions: 68 per minute. Fairness: short=1.08, long=1.62.
- Notes: tail improved further but throughput and headroom loss increased. Need to tune eviction threshold. Observed microburst response slightly worse (higher p95 for bursts) because eviction churn interferes with batching coherence.

Burst scenario (500 rps for 30s):
- Baseline p99 spiked to 2.1s. Variant A: 1.4s. Variant B: 1.1s but with throughput drop and more tail variance immediately after burst.

Microburst trains (100ms pulses):
- Both token-budget variants improved short-request p99 in steady arrivals but were less robust for microbursts in the aggressive mode — the overhead of preempt/requeue amplified latency variance for the very short pulses. Hypothesis: preemption cost (repackaging + cache warm misses) dominates when arrival coherence is tight.

Tracing observations (span-level):
- Preempted requests show +6–12ms median requeue cost (serialization + queue hop).
- Eviction often led to cache disruption for KV-cache-backed decoders for long jobs; we saw small increases in token-generation variance for those evicted items.

Open issues and questions:
- Estimation error: client-provided estimated_token_budget is noisy. We experimented with server-side crude estimator (prompt tokens * 1.5 + warmup delta) which improved correctness but added CPU cost. Should we invest more in a small estimator microservice or rely on client hints?
- Preemption policy complexity: eviction helps short latency but increases churn. Is there a middle ground: soft-shed (reduce token slice) instead of full eviction?
- Interaction with KV cache: evicting long jobs that have warm KV cache hurts their downstream generation time more than expected. Need to detect cache-warmed requests and avoid evicting them.
- Fairness tradeoff: long jobs see bigger slowdown. For enterprise customers doing longer chat sessions this may be undesirable. Consider per-customer budget pools or SLA-aware pinning.

Next experiments planned:
- Variant C: soft-slice preemption — instead of evicting, cap token contribution per-request to a max-per-batch token slice and allow multiple turns (interleaving generation across batches) to amortize preemption cost.
- Variant D: budget-feedback loop — dynamically tune per-request budget multipliers based on observed solo-latency vs queued-latency.
- Test with real client traces (prod anonymized trace from Oct 2024) to validate on realistic patterns.
- Run long-duration soak (48h) to measure tail stability and fairness drift.

Operational runbook notes (temporary):
- Feature gates: token-budgetging is gated under flag EXP_TOKEN_BUDGET on node config. Telemetry added to monitoring: budget_violation_count, preempt_requeues, avg_token_slice_per_batch, budget_fault_rate.
- Quick rollback: disable flag + drain nodes (no code rollback required for prototype).

Random field notes / TODOs:
- Check whether per-client session tagging helps: clients with continuous chat might be allowed soft exceptions.
- Investigate hybrid approach with admission + adaptive batching window where window shortens when many small requests arrive.
- Put together a short doc for product on impact to SLAs and pricing — if p99 improves for interactive flows we can market performance but must be transparent about potential added latency for long-run jobs.

Conclusion (current stance):
- Token-budget backpressure is promising for improving short-request tail latency in mixed workloads with modest throughput cost. Conservative settings (Variant A) seem to hit a good balance; aggressive policies require more engineering to reduce eviction churn and KV-cache disruption. Next step: prototype soft-slice preemption and rerun microburst tests.

-- Maya

(Notes to self: keep this doc as a lab journal. Once we land a stable policy, convert to 'playbook' with CLI knobs and telemetry dashboards.)
